HCI · Privacy & user agency

ConsentDiff at Scale

My contribution
I designed a monthly audit that compares what a site’s privacy policy promises with the choices its consent banner offers.
Research finding
Sites with a visible “Reject all” button scored 0.12 points higher on alignment between policy promises and interface choices.
Role
Sole author
Context
Independent research
Period
2025–2026
Status
CHI Extended Abstracts 2026
OverviewEvidenceMethodNext question

Evidence

Can a visitor act on a policy promise?

I followed 2,400 domains across nine monthly waves. For each snapshot, I compared policy claims with observable choices such as the visibility of rejection and the steps it required.

The audit measures an association between observable interface features and policy alignment. It does not measure whether visitors felt in control.

Read paper Effect sizes in Section 4.2

Research question & method

Do changing privacy interfaces make the choices promised in policy accessible?

As sole author, I developed the longitudinal audit approach connecting policy changes with observable consent-interface behavior. The work brings together semantic clause alignment, interface classification, and a weighted claim–UI alignment measure.

CONCEPTUAL TEASERExpand figure ↗

Method overview (AI-generated) · Monthly snapshots, parallel analysis, and claim–UI alignment.

Monthly snapshots and the alignment score

Privacy is experienced through both policy language and interface actions. ConsentDiff connects these two layers over time, rather than treating a policy document or a consent banner as an isolated snapshot.

  1. Observe over time

    Snapshot sites monthly and align policy clauses semantically to track clause-level changes.

  2. Inspect the interface

    Combine DOM signals and screenshot cues to classify consent-UI patterns.

  3. Connect claims to actions

    Map policy claims to observable predicates and compare alignment across time, regions, and verticals.

Next question

How can longitudinal audits distinguish a clearer interface from a change that truly improves user agency?

Observable interface alignment provides one form of evidence. Understanding whether people can recognize and exercise their choices also calls for user-centered evaluation. This is a proposed extension of the audit.
